newsitem.title: USA: Greenspan sees risks of wage-driven inflation.
newsitem.headline: Greenspan sees risks of wage-driven inflation.

text.p: Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan on Tuesday delivered an upbeat assessment of the U.S. economy but warned of the risks of wage-driven inflation in the future.
In prepared testimony to the Senate Budget Committee, Greenspan said that wages had been held down by heightened job insecurity, but he saw signs that that might be coming to an end.
"The recent pickup in some measures of wages suggest that the transition may be already running its course," the central bank chief added.
Echoing comments made nearly a year ago, he said wages could only be held down so long and would ultimately pick up.
"The important question from a monetary policy point of view is whether prospective labor market conditions will be consistent with the maintenance of satisfactory price performance," he said.
Greenspan said the economy looks to have grown about three percent last year.
"The economy has retained considerable vigor, with few signs of the imbalances and inflationary tensions that have disrupted past expansions," he said.
Greenspan gave the low inflation rate much of the credit for the economy's continued vigor, arguing that it had helped encourage strong capital investment by companies and longer-range planning.
Inflation has partly been held down by stepped-up U.S. imports, which have acted as a "safety valve" for the economy by helping to satisfy domestic private demand, he said.
But the main reason for the low inflation rate, according to Greenspan, is subdued wage growth brought on by heightened job insecurity.

Greenspan acknowledged that other factors may have played a role in keeping inflation down, but he tended to discount their importance. They include the sharp slowdown in health care costs, the declining influence of unions, increased foreign competition, and stepped-up domestic deregulation.

In setting interest rate policy, the central bank needs to take account not of economic conditions now, but those likely to prevail six months to a year ahead, or even longer, Greenspan said. That is because interest rates tend to work with a lag on the economy,

Greenspan, who jolted global stock markets late last year when he warned of the dangers of "irrational exuberance," steered clear of repeating that admonishment on Tuesday, although he did call Wall Street's price rise "breathtakeing."
He said he was encouraged by signs that Americans appear to be investing more of their income, saying they may finally setting aside money needed for retirement.
The Fed chief stressed the importance of increased U.S. savings for the economy as a whole. "Attaining a higher national savings rate quite soon is crucial," he said.
To help boost the national savings rate, Greenspan urged the lawmakers to balance the federal budget and eventually move it into surplus.
As he has done before, the Fed chief threw his support behind those who argue that the consumer price index overstates inflation.
The evidence, he said, is that inflation has been slower and economic growth faster than the government data suggest.
